text: Every KQL query starts with a table name, then reads as a pipeline: each pipe character takes the previous step's result and narrows, reshapes, or summarizes it further. There's no SELECT, no FROM clause buried in the middle — the table comes first, and everything after it transforms what's left. That one habit of reading top to bottom is most of what you need to start writing real queries.

Here's a query you could paste into Log Analytics right now: filter AzureActivity to the last 24 hours, keep only failed operations, group by who did it and what they tried, count each group, and sort the worst offenders to the top. That answers a real question — who's been failing operations on this subscription today — using exactly the control-plane data from last lesson.

Summarize is KQL's aggregation operator, collapsing many rows into one per group, the same job SQL's GROUP BY does. Paired with bin, which rounds a timestamp into fixed buckets, it turns a flood of individual performance-counter rows into a usable time series — average CPU per computer, every five minutes — and render timechart draws that result directly in the editor, with nothing to export first.

The real power shows up once you join tables, because most useful operational questions live in more than one place. This query finds machines that are both running hot on CPU and still reporting in healthy: one side computes high-CPU machines from Perf, the other computes each machine's most recent heartbeat, and join kind=inner keeps only the computers that match on both sides — the same concept as a SQL join, different syntax.

For anything you'll run more than once, a let statement names a reusable value or sub-query at the top of a script, and a query you lean on repeatedly can be saved as a function in the workspace, callable by name from any other query. That same saved query becomes the foundation a scheduled query rule runs on its own cadence, turning a one-off investigation into a standing log-based alert.

That's KQL in practice: a table, a pipeline, summarize and bin for aggregation, render for a quick chart, and join whenever the answer lives in more than one table. Next lesson moves up a layer, into Application Insights — the requests, dependencies, and failure data an actual running application emits, and how to trace one slow request back to its real cause.
